meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Before you diagnose yourself with depression or low self-esteem, first make sure that you are not, in fact, just surrounded by assholes'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Freud, and not William Gibson either. The line began as a 2010 tweet by @debihope; Gibson only retweeted it. Snopes rated the Freud attribution false.

answer.label: Not Sigmund Freud — actually @debihope
answer.authorDates: Twitter user “Notorious d.e.b.” · posted the line 24 January 2010
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the earliest known appearance to a tweet posted by @debihope at 12:23 PM on 24 January 2010; asked about it in 2014, she replied that it “popped right out of my own head and based on a past boyfriend.” The Sigmund Freud Museum in Vienna ↗ lists the saying under “Attributed to Freud, no evidence.”

source.excerpt: Before you diagnose yourself with depression or low self esteem, first make sure you are not, in fact, just surrounded by assholes.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ dates the earliest evidence to a tweet from @debihope timestamped 12:23 PM, 24 January 2010, and reports that when QI contacted her she said it “popped right out of my own head and based on a past boyfriend.” Its conclusion credits the handle @debihope with constructing the saying and states the Freud ascription “has no substantive support.”

The Sigmund Freud Museum in Vienna ↗ lists the line on its quotes page under the heading “Attributed to Freud, no evidence” — a section the museum describes as quotations “attributed to Sigmund Freud but for whose authenticity we have not been able to find any evidence to date.”

The same museum told Snopes there is “no written evidence nor any other reliable source confirming that this would be a Freud quote” and that “the wording speaks against Sigmund Freud,” as reported by Full Fact ↗.
Snopes ↗ reviewed the claim that Freud said it and rated the Freud attribution false (Nur Ibrahim, 23 March 2021).
source.excerptNote: This is the wording Quote Investigator recorded from the original tweet. The viral form drifted: it hyphenates “self-esteem” and inserts “that” before “you are not.” The Freud Museum logs a further-drifted variant reading “depression or an inferiority complex,” and a 2011 Freud-credited version swapped in “jerks.” The account has since been suspended, so the original tweet is no longer live on the platform.
source.rightsNote: No public-domain claim is available here. The line is not Freud's, so it inherits nothing from his long-expired works; its earliest documented appearance is a tweet of 24 January 2010 ↗ by an identifiable author who told Quote Investigator the words were her own — generations after anything that could be public domain by age. Whether US copyright reaches a single sentence this short is a genuinely separate question we do not resolve; what we can say is that nothing about this quote is public domain by age.

misattribution.heading: Three wrong names, one real one
misattribution.intro: This saying has been pinned on two famous men in turn, and each attribution has a traceable cause. Quote Investigator untangled the chain in 2014.

items.why: The line reads as therapeutic advice, so it drifted to the most famous psychoanalyst — but no Freud work, letter, or lecture has ever been produced containing it. The Sigmund Freud Museum in Vienna ↗ lists it under “Attributed to Freud, no evidence,” and Snopes ↗ rated the Freud attribution false. QI is blunt: the ascription “has no substantive support.”

items.scope: The retweet that became an attribution
items.why: The cyberpunk novelist retweeted the line, and the act of retweeting alone produced the linkage ↗. He has denied it repeatedly — “Actually not my quote. Never said it” (8 December 2011) and, in a 2018 tweet quoted by Full Fact ↗, “This is misattributed to me. I didn't write it. It's obviously funny on first glance, but not really smart about depression…” Wikiquote ↗ files it under Misattributed.

Gibson himself pointed at Winterburn (@5tevenw) as the origin. QI's citation record shows Winterburn tweeted matching text on 28 February 2011 — over a year after @debihope — and that this copy was retweeted more than 1,500 times, which is why it looked like the source. Wikiquote states plainly ↗ that Winterburn is not the original creator.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator's conclusion ↗: “based on current evidence QI believes that the twitter handle @debihope should be credited with constructing this saying.” A woman on Twitter wrote a joke about an ex-boyfriend, and the internet handed it to Freud.

context.heading: Why this one landed on Freud
lead: The line is a joke with a clinical frame: it borrows the vocabulary of diagnosis (“depression,” “low self-esteem”) and then pulls the rug out. Quote Investigator makes the mechanism explicit — the expression can be read as therapeutic advice, and so it was reassigned to the most famous psychoanalytic practitioner ↗. A punchline that sounds like therapy drifts toward the man on the couch's other side.

The Freud Museum's objection is not just archival but stylistic: it told Snopes that “the wording speaks against Sigmund Freud,” as reported by Full Fact ↗. Worth adding as a plain observation: Freud wrote in German and died in 1939, so any real Freud line would reach English through a named translator — and no translator, edition, or page has ever been produced for this one.
context.detailsSummary: The retweet chain that erased the author
detailsBody: Quote Investigator's citation record shows the sequence. @debihope tweeted the line on 24 January 2010. More than a year later, on 28 February 2011, Steven Winterburn (@5tevenw) posted matching text; that tweet was retweeted more than 1,500 times and became the version most people saw.

William Gibson was one of the influential retweeters, and QI is careful to note he was not trying to deceive anyone — he was simply sharing it. The act of retweeting alone welded his name to the line. He has been disowning it ever since: on 8 December 2011, “Actually not my quote. Never said it,” and, asked what it was like to have a viral quote misattributed to him, “Very 21st Century.”

The earliest Freud ascription in QI's record is a tweet of 13 October 2011 that credits “Freud” while using the softened word “jerks” — evidence that the attribution and the wording were drifting at the same time.
